q: Which property of an algorithm requires every step to be precise and to have only one meaning?
x: Definiteness means each step is clearly and unambiguously stated. Finiteness is about the algorithm stopping after a limited number of steps.

q: Which is the best description of an algorithm?
o: A program written in a high-level language
A diagram of the parts of a computer
Any list of steps, even one that never ends
A finite sequence of clear steps that solves a problem
x: An algorithm is a finite, well-defined set of steps for solving a problem, and it can be written in any form, not only as a program. A list of steps that never ends fails finiteness.

q: A problem to which every problem in NP can be reduced in polynomial time, but which need not itself be in NP, is called:
x: That is the definition of NP-hard. NP-complete problems are the NP-hard problems that are also in NP, so "need not be in NP" points to NP-hard.

q:
For a large `n`, what is the time complexity of this code?
```
for i in range(n):
    print(i)
for j in range(10):
    print(j)
```
x: The first loop runs n times and the second a fixed 10 times, one after the other, so the work is n + 10 steps, which grows like O(n). The loops are not nested, so it is not O(n²).

q:
For a large `n`, how does the number of passes of this loop grow?
```
i = 1
while i < n:
    i = i * 2
```
x: i doubles each pass (1, 2, 4, 8, …), so it reaches n after about log₂ n passes: O(log n). It would be O(n) only if i went up by 1 each pass.

q: Finding the shortest road route from Lahore to Peshawar, out of all possible routes, is which type of computational problem?
x: The task is to pick the best (shortest) of many possible answers, which makes it an optimisation problem. A decision problem would only ask a yes/no question, such as whether a route under 200 km exists.

q: If someone found a polynomial-time algorithm for one NP-complete problem, what would follow?
o: Every problem in NP could be solved in polynomial time
Only that one problem would move into P
The halting problem would become solvable
Every NP-complete problem would become unsolvable
x: Every NP problem reduces to any NP-complete problem in polynomial time, so a fast algorithm for one would give fast algorithms for all of NP (P = NP). The halting problem is unsolvable whatever happens to NP.

q: Reading the element at a given index of a Python list, such as `L[500]`, takes the same time however long the list is. What is its time complexity?
x: A fixed amount of work, not depending on n, is constant time, O(1). Indexing does not walk through the elements one by one, which would be O(n).

q: Coins of Rs 1, Rs 3 and Rs 4 are available in any number. A greedy method pays Rs 6 by always taking the largest coin that does not exceed the amount still to pay. How many coins does it use?
x: Greedy first takes 4 (2 left), then cannot take 3 or 4, so takes 1 and 1: three coins. Greedy does not look ahead, so it misses the better answer 3 + 3; there is no Rs 2 coin for 4 + 2.

q: Algorithm X takes n² steps and algorithm Y takes 100n steps on an input of size n. For n = 50, which takes fewer steps?
o: Y, because an O(n) algorithm always takes fewer steps
Both take the same number of steps
x: X: 50² = 2,500; Y: 100 × 50 = 5,000, so X is faster here. Big-O describes growth for large n: Y wins only when n > 100, not for every n.

q: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort on n elements?
x: In the worst case bubble sort makes about n passes of about n comparisons each, so O(n²). O(n log n) is merge sort's complexity.

q: Which statement about searching an unsorted list of 500 names is true?
o: Binary search works on it; linear search needs it sorted first
Linear search works on it; binary search needs it sorted first
Both methods need the list sorted first
Neither method can be used until it is sorted
x: Linear search checks every element in turn, so the order does not matter. Binary search discards half the list after each comparison, which is valid only if the list is sorted.

q: Selection sort (descending): each pass finds the largest value in the unsorted part and swaps it with the first unsorted position. What is `[3, 8, 2, 6, 5]` after two passes?
x: Pass 1: largest 8 swaps with 3 → [8, 3, 2, 6, 5]. Pass 2: largest of [3, 2, 6, 5] is 6, which swaps with 3 → [8, 6, 2, 3, 5]. [8, 3, 2, 6, 5] is after one pass only.

q: Bubble sort (ascending) goes left to right and swaps each adjacent pair whose left value is larger. How many swaps does it make in the first full pass on `[4, 2, 5, 1, 3]`?
x: 4 > 2 swap → [2, 4, 5, 1, 3]; 4 < 5 no swap; 5 > 1 swap → [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]; 5 > 3 swap → [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]. Three swaps; 4 is the number of comparisons, not swaps.

q: Linear search is used on a list of 8 elements, and the target value is not in the list. How many comparisons does it make?
x: To be sure the value is absent, linear search must compare it with every element: 8 comparisons. 3 is roughly what binary search would need on a sorted list.

q: Why does binary search need far fewer comparisons than linear search on a long sorted list?
o: Each comparison removes about half of the remaining elements
It compares two elements at a time instead of one
It starts from the last element instead of the first
It sorts the list again while searching
x: Comparing with the middle element tells binary search which half can hold the target, so the part left to search halves each step (about log₂ n steps). It still makes one comparison at a time.
lo = 0, hi = 5, mid = 2: 7 < 13, so lo = 3. mid = (3 + 5) // 2 = 4: L[4] is 13, so it returns 4. The function returns the index, not the value 13; 5 would be counting positions from 1.

q:
What is printed?
```
L = [7, 4, 9, 2, 8]
m = 0
for i in range(1, len(L)):
    if L[i] < L[m]:
        m = i
L[0], L[m] = L[m], L[0]
print(L)
```
x: The loop finds the index of the smallest value, m = 3 (the value 2), and the last line swaps it with L[0]: [2, 4, 9, 7, 8]. This is one selection-sort pass, so the list is not fully sorted.

q: Merge sort keeps splitting a list of 8 elements into halves until every part has a single element. How many levels of splitting are there (8 → 4 + 4 is the first level)?
x: 8 → 4 + 4 (level 1) → four parts of 2 (level 2) → eight parts of 1 (level 3); log₂ 8 = 3. 7 is the number of separate split operations, not levels.

q: Which of these sorting methods makes at most n − 1 swaps on any list of n elements?
o: Insertion sort done by swapping neighbours
Bubble sort with an early stop
x: Selection sort makes at most one swap per pass and needs n − 1 passes. Bubble sort (with or without early stop) and neighbour-swapping insertion sort can need about n²/2 swaps on a reversed list.

q: Insertion sort (descending) takes each element from the left and inserts it into its place in the sorted part before it, largest first. Starting with `[3, 7, 5, 9]`, what is the list just after 5 has been inserted?
x: Inserting 7 before 3 gives [7, 3, 5, 9]; then 5 goes between 7 and 3: [7, 5, 3, 9]. 9 has not been inserted yet, so the fully sorted [9, 7, 5, 3] comes one step later.

q: Binary search looks for 12 in `[5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35]` (indexes 0 to 6), using middle index = (low + high) // 2 and stopping when low > high. Which values are compared with 12, in order?
x: mid = 3 (20): 12 < 20, high = 2. mid = 1 (10): 12 > 10, low = 2. mid = 2 (15): 12 < 15, high = 1. Now low > high, so 12 is not found after comparing 20, 10, 15. Stopping after 10 misses the last check.

q: A bubble sort (ascending) makes left-to-right passes of adjacent swaps and stops after the first pass that makes no swap. How many passes does it make on `[1, 2, 3, 5, 4]`?
x: Pass 1 swaps 5 and 4, giving [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The list is now sorted, but the algorithm only knows this after pass 2 makes no swap, so it makes 2 passes. 4 is the count without the early stop.

q: Binary search, with middle index = (low + high) // 2, is wrongly used on the unsorted list `[9, 2, 7, 4, 5]` to look for 2. What is the result?
o: It reports 2 as not found, although 2 is in the list
It finds 2 after checking every element
It sorts the list first and then finds 2
x: mid = 2 (7): 2 < 7, so high = 1. mid = 0 (9): 2 < 9, so high = −1, and low > high ends the search. Index 1 is never checked, so the search fails; binary search does not sort the list itself.

q: The Undo feature of a text editor undoes the most recent change first. Which data structure suits it best?
x: The last change made is the first one undone, which is last in, first out: a stack. A queue would undo the oldest change first.

q: In a tree, what is the node that has no parent called?
x: The root is the top node and the only one with no parent. A leaf is a node with no children.

q: A graph in which every edge has a direction, such as a map of one-way roads, is called:
x: When each edge goes one way only (from one vertex to another), the graph is directed. In an undirected graph each edge can be followed both ways.

q: A stack can hold at most 3 values. Starting empty: push 1, push 2, pop, push 3, push 4, push 5. What happens?
o: All pushes succeed; the stack holds 1, 3, 4 and 5
The last push causes overflow, as the stack already holds 1, 3 and 4
x: After push 1, push 2, pop the stack holds 1; push 3 and push 4 fill it to 1, 3, 4. Pushing 5 onto a full stack is overflow. The pop is safe (underflow is popping an empty stack).

q: Ali, Bina and Hamid join an empty queue at a bank counter, in that order. One customer is served, then Dawood joins, then two customers are served. Who is now in the queue?
x: A queue serves first in, first out: Ali leaves first; Dawood joins at the rear behind Bina and Hamid; Bina and Hamid are served next, leaving Dawood. "Ali only" is what a stack (last in, first out) would leave.

q: In a tree, R is the root with children S and T; S has children U and V; V has one child, W. How many leaf nodes does the tree have?
x: A leaf has no children: U, W and T are leaves, so 3. V is not a leaf because it has the child W; counting V gives the wrong answer 4.

q: The values 30, 10, 45, 5, 20, 40 are inserted, in that order, into an empty binary search tree (smaller values go left, larger go right). What is its in-order traversal (left subtree, node, right subtree)?
x: The in-order traversal of a binary search tree always lists its values in ascending order: 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 45. 30, 10, 5, 20, 45, 40 is the pre-order traversal of the same tree.

q: The values 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 are inserted, in that order, into an empty binary search tree. When the tree is searched for 60, which nodes are compared, in order?
x: 60 > 50, so go right to 70; 60 < 70, so go left, reaching 60. A BST search follows one path from the root and never visits 30, which is in the left subtree.

q: An undirected graph has vertices P, Q, R, S and edges P–Q, Q–R, R–S, S–P and P–R. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
x: Degrees: P 3, Q 2, R 3, S 2, total 10. Every edge touches two vertices, so the sum is always twice the number of edges (2 × 5); 5 is the number of edges itself.

q: Why is adding a new first element quicker in a linked list than at the start of an array-style list?
o: A linked list keeps its elements sorted
Only a few links change; no existing element has to be shifted
A linked list stores all its elements in one block of memory
A linked list can be searched with binary search
x: The new node just points to the old first node and becomes the head. In an array every existing element must move one place to make room. It is the array, not the linked list, that uses one block of memory.

q: A map app stores cities and the roads between them; a city may be linked to many others, and roads can form loops. Which data structure suits it best?
x: A graph allows any vertex to connect to any other, including cycles. A tree has no cycles and gives each node only one parent, so it cannot model loops of roads.

q: A program checks the brackets in `( [ ] ( ) )` from left to right with a stack: each opening bracket is pushed, and each closing bracket pops its matching opening bracket. What is the largest number of brackets on the stack at any one time?
x: ( push (1), [ push (2), ] pop (1), ( push (2), ) pop (1), ) pop (0). The stack never holds more than 2. 3 is the number of opening brackets, but they are never all on the stack together.

q: An undirected graph has edges P–Q, P–R, Q–S, R–S and S–T. A depth-first traversal starts at P; from each vertex it goes to the first unvisited neighbour in alphabetical order, and goes back only when there is none. In what order are the vertices visited?
x: P → Q (first neighbour) → S (Q's only unvisited one) → R (S's first unvisited one); R has no unvisited neighbours, so go back to S → T. P, Q, R, S, T is the breadth-first order.

q: A postfix expression is worked out with a stack: each number is pushed, and each operator pops two values (the first one popped is the right-hand operand) and pushes the result. What is the value of `6 2 / 3 4 * +`?
x: 6, 2 pushed; / gives 6 / 2 = 3. 3, 4 pushed; * gives 12. + pops 12 and 3 and gives 15. 12 forgets that the first result, 3, is still on the stack.

q: In logic, which symbol stands for disjunction ("or")?
x: ∨ is "or" (disjunction). ∧ is "and" (conjunction), ¬ is "not" and → is "if … then".

q: When is p ∧ q true?
o: When at least one of p and q is true
When p and q have the same truth value
When p is true and q is false
When p and q are both true
x: A conjunction is true only when both parts are true. "At least one true" describes p ∨ q, and "same truth value" describes p ↔ q.

q: p: "It is raining." q: "The ground is wet." Which sentence is the converse of p → q?
o: If it is not raining, then the ground is not wet.
If the ground is wet, then it is raining.
If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining.
It is raining and the ground is wet.
x: The converse swaps the two parts: q → p. "If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining" is ¬q → ¬p, the contrapositive.

q: For p = T, q = F and r = T, what are the values of (p → q) ∨ ¬r and (p ∨ q) ∧ r, in that order?
x: p → q is T → F = F and ¬r = F, so F ∨ F = F. p ∨ q = T and r = T, so T ∧ T = T.

q: Which of these is a contradiction (false in every row of its truth table)?
x: p and ¬p can never both be true, so p ∧ ¬p is always false. p ∨ ¬p and p → p are always true (tautologies), and p ∧ q is true when both are true.

q: To work out travel time, a route-planning program keeps only each road's length and speed limit and ignores details such as the colour of road signs. Which computational thinking skill is this?
x: Keeping the details that matter and leaving out the rest is abstraction. Decomposition would mean breaking the problem into smaller sub-problems.

q: In how many of the 4 rows of its truth table (for p and q) is (p → q) ∧ ¬p true?
x: ¬p is true only when p = F, and then p → q is true whatever q is. So the rows p = F, q = T and p = F, q = F make it true: 2 rows. When p = T, ¬p is false.

q: Rule: ∀x (E(x) → M(x)), where E(x) means "x is an engineer" and M(x) means "x knows maths". Fact: E(Sana). What can be concluded?
o: Every person who knows maths is an engineer
x: The rule holds for every x, so it holds for Sana: E(Sana) → M(Sana). With E(Sana) true, modus ponens gives M(Sana). The rule does not say that everyone who knows maths is an engineer.

q: The domain is all people. S(x) means "x is a student" and L(x) means "x likes chess". Which formula says "Some students like chess"?
x: We need at least one x who is a student and likes chess: ∃x (S(x) ∧ L(x)). ∃x (S(x) → L(x)) is already true if any one person is not a student, so it does not say what is meant.

q: Which expression is equivalent to ¬(p → q)?
x: p → q is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q; by De Morgan, ¬(¬p ∨ q) = p ∧ ¬q. This is right because p → q is false only when p is true and q is false. ¬p ∨ q is p → q itself.
